stem: During a B.E. F.A.S.T. check, both arms are raised and one arm drifts downward. Which of the following interpretations is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: This excludes stroke because both arms moved
options.misconception: Any movement is being treated as reassurance despite asymmetric arm drift.
options.explanation: The CDC specifically identifies one arm drifting downward during the arm test as a stroke warning sign.

options.label: B
options.text: This matters only when both arms drift
options.misconception: The one-sided nature of the warning sign is being reversed.
options.explanation: The cited B.E. F.A.S.T. test asks whether one arm drifts downward; bilateral drift is not required.

options.label: C
options.text: This is reassuring if speech remains clear
options.misconception: One normal component is being used to dismiss a different positive stroke sign.
options.explanation: The CDC directs action when any of the listed face, arm, or speech signs is present, not only when all appear together.

options.label: D
options.text: This is a stroke warning sign; call 9-1-1
options.misconception: None; unilateral arm drift is a positive B.E. F.A.S.T. sign.
options.explanation: One arm drifting downward is the arm finding in the CDC B.E. F.A.S.T. check. Seeing this sign should prompt an immediate emergency call.

options.label: E
options.text: Wait unless facial droop appears later
options.misconception: Urgent action is being postponed until a second warning sign develops.
options.explanation: The CDC says to call right away if any of these signs is seen; waiting for facial droop delays care.

context: Learning objective: apply the arm component of B.E. F.A.S.T. One arm drifting downward is a positive stroke warning sign; a single positive component is enough to activate emergency help.
